name: Knee-Smart Strength & Conditioning: Build, Burn, Move Better
rationale:
This program is built around three things at once: dropping body fat, adding real muscle, and building your engine for conditioning — all while keeping a right knee with arthritis pain-free and getting stronger, not more irritated. You train five days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sun) in a pattern of lower body, upper body, full-body power, upper body again, then a dedicated aerobic day, so no muscle group is ever hit on truly consecutive high-strain days even when the calendar days are back-to-back. Monday and Tuesday work opposite halves of the body so one doesn't compromise the other; Thursday's full-body power session sits two full days after your last leg work so your knee has recovered before it takes hip-hinge and pressing load again; Friday shifts the upper-body angle so nothing repeats stale; Sunday is pure aerobic work plus easy core, which does double duty as both fat-loss engine work and active recovery before the next week's lifting starts. Across the 8-12 weeks the program runs in 4-week blocks — the first four weeks build your base strength and work capacity, and the last week of each block (except the very final one) is an automatic deload where volume drops by around 40% and the intensity target eases off; that's not a step backward, it's how your body actually absorbs the training and comes back stronger for the next block, so don't skip it or push through it.

The engine behind this is simple: to build muscle and burn fat, your body needs a repeated mechanical stress (lifting near-maximal loads for moderate reps) that signals muscle fibers to grow, combined with an energy deficit created partly by the conditioning pieces and the general calorie cost of more muscle mass at rest. Heavy compound lifts (deadlift variations, presses, rows) come first in every session while you're fresh, because that's when you can handle the load that actually drives strength adaptation; accessories and short conditioning bursts come after because they finish off the muscle without compromising the main lift. For your knee, arthritis means the joint doesn't like grinding through deep, loaded flexion repeatedly, so every squat pattern here is range-limited (a pin squat catches you at a set depth instead of going deep) and hip-hinge movements like the trap bar deadlift and Romanian deadlift do more of the heavy lifting instead — you still get full lower-body strength work, just through a joint-friendlier path. Every single day also opens with two knee-specific activation drills (terminal knee extension work, an isometric wall-sit style hold) done light and pain-free — if anything pinches, stop that drill and check with a physio, this is prep, not treatment. The real trade-off here is that with only five days and a knee to manage, I prioritized joint-friendly strength and short conditioning bursts over any high-impact jumping or sprinting work — you'll still get real conditioning gains from kettlebells, sleds, ski erg, and steady rowing, just without the pounding.

name: MMA Strength, Power & Conditioning — 3-Day Fight Prep
rationale:
This program is built for a competing MMA fighter with advanced training experience who needs three things at once: raw strength, explosive power, and the ability to repeat hard efforts round after round. With only three training days, each session is built as a full package rather than splitting qualities across more days than you have: Monday is a lower-body strength and power day (the hip and leg drive behind takedowns, sprawls and kicks), Wednesday is an upper-body strength and power day (the pressing and pulling strength behind clinch work and striking), and Saturday is a full-body explosive and conditioning day that trains rotational power and short, repeated-effort capacity the way a fight actually demands it. The whole plan runs as three 4-week blocks. Within each block the loads and effort climb week to week, and the app will automatically back off volume by about 40% and ease the difficulty target on the last week of the first two blocks — that's the deload, and it's there on purpose, not a sign anything went wrong. The final block runs straight through at full intensity since there's no event to taper for, so that's where you should expect to hit your best numbers.

The reasoning behind the layout comes down to how each quality is actually built. Heavy compound lifts like the trap bar deadlift, front squat, bench press and barbell row drive maximal strength through better nervous-system recruitment of muscle fibers and thickening of the fibers themselves — this is the base everything else sits on. Explosive work like trap bar jumps, power cleans, med ball throws and landmine rotations trains rate of force development — how fast you can turn strength into force — through what's called the stretch-shortening cycle, the spring-like effect of muscle and tendon loading and releasing quickly; this is what actually shows up as faster hands and a heavier kick, not just a bigger squat number. Short, hard conditioning pieces like sled pushes, battle ropes and ski erg intervals train your ability to produce repeated high-output bursts and clear the metabolic fatigue that builds up during them, which mirrors the stop-start nature of rounds far better than slow steady cardio would. Explosive work is placed before heavy lifting in every session because it needs a fresh nervous system to be trained well, and heavy lifting comes before accessories for the same reason. The trade-off, given only three days a week, is that you don't get dedicated days for each quality in isolation — instead each session blends strength, power and conditioning, while the 48-72 hours between sessions gives an advanced lifter enough recovery to keep loading hard without breaking down. The deload weeks exist to let your joints and nervous system catch up on that accumulated fatigue before the next block asks for more, which is what keeps you progressing instead of stalling or getting hurt.

name: MMA Strength, Power & Fight Conditioning — 3-Day Split
rationale:
This program is built to make you hit harder, move faster, and hold up for five rounds, using three sessions a week since that's what your schedule allows: Monday hits lower-body strength and power (the base for takedowns, sprawls, and leg drive on strikes), Wednesday hits upper-body pressing and pulling strength (clinch work, punching power, grappling control), and Friday is a full-body explosive and fight-conditioning session that ties rotational power, Olympic-lift-style explosiveness, and short high-intensity bursts together — the closest thing to fight pace you'll do in the weight room. The spacing works in your favor: two days between Monday and Wednesday, two more before Friday, then three clear days before the cycle repeats, so no muscle group ever gets hit hard twice without real recovery. Across the 12 weeks you'll run three 4-week blocks; the load and complexity build within each block, and the last week of the first two blocks is an automatic lighter week (roughly 40% less volume, easier target intensity) so your joints and nervous system catch up before you push the numbers again — the final block has no deload because there's nothing after it to prepare for.

The physiology is straightforward: heavy compound lifts (squat, deadlift, press, row) 1-2 times a week per movement pattern is the proven dose for building maximal strength, because it's mechanical tension on the muscle-tendon unit that drives the nervous system to recruit more motor units and the muscle to add contractile tissue — you need enough of it to force adaptation but not so much that you can't recover on three days a week.

name: Six Month Strength and Power Program
rationale: XPerformance six-month strength and power program, Sep 28 2026 to Mar 28 2027. Six mesocycles: volume building, intensification, absolute strength, high velocity loading, speed strength, peaking. Four S&C days a week, two hard and two easy, each finishing with tissue-capacity work. The 8-10 movement ceiling includes main work, accessories, sprints and tendon finishers; easy days stay at eight. Hard days 65-80 min plus Monday aerobic; easy days 25-35 min plus aerobic. Currently loaded with BLOCK 1 WEEK 1 numbers. The dated weekly tables for weeks 2-26 are in the source document and go in once per-week prescriptions are supported.
